title: University of Cambridge NERC-Funded PhD Studentships 2027: 15 Fully Funded CREATES Doctoral Opportunities in Environmental Science
summary: The University of Cambridge is offering 15 NERC-funded PhD studentships for students starting in October 2027 through the Cambridge Research Experience and Advanced Training for Environmental Scientists (CREATES) Doctoral Landscape Award (DLA) . Each studentship is designed to support 3.5 years of doctoral research in environmental science, with research opportunities hosted across relevant University of Cambridge departments and the British Antarctic Survey. The CREATES programme is the University of Cambridge s new environmental science doctoral training programme under the Natural Environment Research Council (NERC) Doctoral Landscape Awards . It succeeds the previous C-CLEAR programme and is designed to develop researchers working across major environmental challenges, including climate change, biodiversity, conservation, Earth sciences and environmental processes. For prospective PhD students interested in environmental research, climate science, conservation, geology, biodiversity, environmental modelling, plant sciences, zoology, archaeology and related areas, the 2027 CREATES DLA provides an opportunity to pursue doctoral study at Cambridge while being considered for NERC funding. University of Cambridge CREATES NERC PhD Studentships 2027 The Cambridge Research Experience and Advanced Training for Environmental Scientists (CREATES) is built around interdisciplinary environmental science research. The programme brings together the University of Cambridge and the British Antarctic Survey as hosts and works with a wider network of partners from areas including government, industry and the third sector. The programme addresses environmental challenges that have major implications for society, including: Climate change and environmental change Biodiversity loss Conservation Food production and land-use pressures Environmental and natural hazards Earth-system processes Polar and cryospheric science Environmental modelling and informatics Ecosystem processes Evolutionary and ecological research The CREATES programme is organised around three broad research themes: Solid Earth and Geological Hazards Climate Change and Environmental Processes Biology and Conservation These themes reflect the breadth of environmental research available through the programme. What Does the NERC-Funded PhD Opportunity Offer? For students beginning their studies in October 2027, Cambridge will offer: 15 NERC-funded PhD studentships 3.5 years of doctoral funding Research opportunities across eligible Cambridge departments and the British Antarctic Survey Access to the CREATES doctoral training environment Interdisciplinary environmental science training Opportunities to work with supervisors whose research aligns with NERC s remit Development of research, professional, technical and transferable skills The official programme states that the 2027 studentships will form part of a five-cohort CREATES programme replacing the previous C-CLEAR doctoral training programme. The wider CREATES programme also connects students with collaborative partners, providing opportunities for networking, professional development and, where applicable, internships and partner-led activities. Research Areas and Departments One of the major features of the CREATES DLA is the range of environmental research areas available to applicants. Current CREATES supervisors are associated with departments and research environments including: Department of Archaeology British Antarctic Survey Department of Chemistry Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics Department of Earth Sciences Department of Genetics Department of Geography Department of Plant Sciences Scott Polar Research Institute Department of Zoology This means prospective applicants can approach the programme from different academic backgrounds, provided their proposed research fits within the relevant environmental science and NERC remit. Examples of Potential Research Areas The current supervisor directory includes research areas such as: Climate and climate change Atmospheric science Ocean circulation Polar physical oceanography Palaeoenvironments Palaeobiology Conservation ecology Ecosystem-scale processes Environmental informatics Evolutionary biology Population genetics Behavioural ecology Marine ecology Plant and crop science Environmental physiology Geochemistry Volcanology Geological hazards Earth-surface processes Environmental microbiology Archaeology Quaternary science Cryosphere and climate research Applicants should examine the current supervisor and topic information carefully because the specific research interests and available supervision areas vary between academics. How the CREATES Research Topics Work An important feature of this PhD opportunity is that applicants are not necessarily applying to a completely finalised PhD project title . Instead, applicants are expected to identify topics and supervisors that particularly interest them. The final research project can then be developed with the supervisory team during the first term of doctoral study. This means applicants should focus on demonstrating: Their research interests Their understanding of the relevant environmental research area Why the topic interests them Which supervisors they would like to work with How their academic background relates to the proposed area Their potential to undertake independent doctoral research The programme strongly recommends contacting prospective supervisors before submitting an application. This allows applicants and supervisors to explore whether their research interests are compatible and can also provide useful advice about the application. What If a Prospective Supervisor Does Not Respond? The programme recognises that contacting academics can sometimes be difficult, particularly if a potential supervisor is conducting fieldwork or otherwise unavailable. Applicants who are interested in a particular area but cannot establish contact with a suitable supervisor can contact the CREATES DLA Administrator, who can help connect them with an academic. The administrator can be contacted at: dtp-admin@esc.cam.ac.uk NERC Research Remit Requirement Applicants seeking CREATES NERC DLA funding must ensure that at least one of their proposed research topics falls within the NERC research remit . Applicants may identify projects or research areas that fall under other UK Research Councils, but they will only be considered for CREATES DLA funding if at least one proposed subject area fits within NERC s remit. If admitted and funded through the DLA, the research topic must continue to remain within that remit during the development of the project. This makes it particularly important for applicants to understand the environmental science focus of NERC before selecting their preferred research topics. Cambridge PhD Admission Requirements Before applying for the NERC funding, applicants must first ensure that they meet the University s requirements for admission to the relevant PhD programme. According to the CREATES application guidance, applicants are expected to have: 1. A Strong Relevant Degree Applicants should normally have at least a 2.1 Honours degree from a UK university , or an equivalent qualification from an overseas university. The guidance gives CGPA 3.5/4.0 as an example of an equivalent overseas academic standard, although applicants should check the specific requirements applicable to their circumstances and chosen course. 2. Two Outstanding References Applicants need to provide two outstanding references . The programme recommends requesting references well in advance of the application deadline so that referees have enough time to prepare and submit them. 3. English-Language Proficiency Applicants must meet the University s English-language requirements. The exact evidence required can depend on the applicant s circumstances, previous education and course, so prospective international applicants should consult Cambridge s official English-language requirements before submitting their application. How to Apply for the Cambridge CREATES NERC PhD Applicants must apply through the University of Cambridge Applicant Portal and select the PhD course relevant to their preferred supervisor. The application process involves several important stages. Step 1: Research Supervisors and Topics Begin by examining the available CREATES topics and supervisors. Applicants are encouraged to: Identify research areas that match their interests. Review potential supervisors research interests. Identify more than one suitable topic where appropriate. Contact prospective supervisors. Discuss research interests and potential project directions. Develop a prioritised list of preferred supervisors and topics. The programme recommends providing a prioritised list because academic staff can act as lead supervisor for only one CREATES studentship per application round. Applicants may also identify supervisors in different departments. Step 2: Check the NERC Remit At least one proposed topic must fit within NERC s remit if the applicant wants to be considered for CREATES DLA funding. Step 3: Apply for the Relevant Cambridge PhD The application must be submitted through Cambridge s Applicant Portal. Applicants should select: Michaelmas Term 2027 start — 1 October 2027. Step 4: Request Funding Consideration When the application asks: “Do you wish to apply for funding?” applicants should select: “Yes — I wish to apply for funding.” Applicants should also indicate that they wish to be considered for the NERC Doctoral Landscape Award and identify their preferred CREATES topics and supervisors. Research Summary Required for the Application Applicants seeking DLA funding will need to provide information about their planned research interests. This includes: Prospective supervisor or supervisors Proposed topic or topics A 250-word summary of the area or areas of research they are interested in Some Cambridge departments may request a longer research proposal as part of their own admissions process, but the CREATES DLA specifically focuses on the applicant s 250-word research-interest summary. Applicants should therefore make sure that their 250-word summary is focused, relevant to NERC s remit and clearly connected to the research interests of their preferred supervisors. Where Should Applicants Enter Their Research Information? The exact structure of the Cambridge application form varies depending on the department and course. Applicants may encounter sections such as: Research Other Information Course-Specific Questions Additional Information to Support Your Application If a Research section is available, applicants should use it to provide information about their proposed supervisors, topics and research summary. If the Research section is not available, applicants should look for research-related questions under Course-Specific Questions . The Additional Information to Support Your Application section can also be used where applicants need more space to explain their preferred combinations of topics and supervisors. Applicants Should Complete the Entire Cambridge Application The CREATES guidance emphasises that the instructions concerning topics, supervisors and the 250-word summary do not replace the other questions in the University s PhD application. Applicants should answer all other questions required by their chosen Cambridge course. The funding section should also clearly indicate the applicant s interest in NERC funding and include preferred supervisors where requested. Funding and Financial Support The CREATES opportunity is a NERC-funded PhD studentship . The 2027 call provides 15 studentships, each lasting 3.5 years. The current Cambridge CREATES funding information explains that NERC studentships can cover tuition and provide a maintenance allowance and Research Training Support Grant. It also states that a limited number of studentships can be offered to international students, with UKRI funding covering the UK-rate fees, maintenance allowance and Research Training Support Grant; Cambridge has agreed to waive the difference between international and home fees for DLA students. Applicants should check the latest funding guidance for the precise conditions applying to the 2027 intake. International applicants should also note that certain expenses, such as visa and health-related surcharges, may not be covered by the DLA funding itself. Cambridge recommends that international applicants also consider other funding opportunities where appropriate. Important Application Deadlines The CREATES NERC DLA deadline is tied directly to the funding deadline for the applicant s chosen Cambridge course. For the 2027 entry cycle, the relevant deadline will be either 8 December 2026 or 6 January 2027 , depending on the course. Applicants must check the deadline for their first-choice course carefully. The final CREATES DLA deadline is therefore: 8 December 2026 or 6 January 2027, depending on the chosen Cambridge course. All supporting documentation, including references, must be submitted by the applicable deadline. Applicants should not assume that every Cambridge department uses the same deadline. Earlier Funding Deadlines Some other Cambridge funding schemes may have earlier deadlines. The CREATES guidance specifically highlights: The Department of Chemistry may have an earlier deadline for other PhD funding. The Department of Geography may have an earlier deadline for other PhD funding. US-based applicants seeking Gates Cambridge funding should apply by 14 October 2026, including references. Applicants interested in multiple funding sources should therefore research each relevant funding deadline rather than relying solely on the CREATES deadline. CREATES 2027 Application Timeline The programme has provided the following expected timeline for the 2027 intake: Supervisor Information Supervisor pages for the 2027 entry cycle were scheduled to be updated by: 1 September 2026 Application Deadline Depending on the selected course: 8 December 2026 or 6 January 2027 All supporting documents and references must be submitted by the relevant deadline. Interviews Online interviews are anticipated to take place during the week of: 22 February 2027 Offers Initial offers are expected to begin being communicated in late February 2027. The NERC Universal Acceptance Date is: Noon, 17 March 2027 What Does the CREATES Programme Look For in Applicants? Beyond minimum admission requirements, the CREATES DLA assessment process considers several aspects of a candidate s potential. The programme s assessment framework includes: Academic Excellence Applicants are assessed on factors such as: Degree results or predicted results Achievement in relevant subjects Academic achievements Research experience Evidence of advanced knowledge in the proposed research area Awareness of knowledge gaps and relevant methodologies Originality and Independence The programme looks for evidence of: Independent working ability Self-motivation Problem-solving Critical decision-making Independence during research or project work Communication Skills Applicants should be able to: Communicate clearly Explain complex ideas logically Provide precise and detailed answers Demonstrate enthusiasm for environmental science Preparedness for Doctoral Study The assessment also considers: Intellectual curiosity Ability to evaluate personal strengths and weaknesses Awareness of skills gaps Ability to identify challenges Ability to develop strategies for overcoming challenges Understanding of how doctoral study fits into future career plans Importantly, CREATES states that contextual information can also be taken into account. This can include adversity, caring responsibilities, employment undertaken alongside study, and differences in access to research opportunities. Why Contacting a Supervisor Before Applying Matters A strong supervisor match is an important part of the CREATES application process. Because applicants are expected to identify potential research areas and supervisors, contacting academics before applying can help applicants: Understand whether their research interests align. Learn more about potential projects. Discuss possible research directions. Determine whether a supervisor is accepting students. Decide which topics to prioritise. Develop a more focused research-interest statement. The programme itself strongly advises applicants to contact prospective supervisors before submitting an application. How to Prepare a Strong CREATES Application Applicants can begin preparing well before the deadline. 1. Research the Supervisors Read the profiles of potential supervisors carefully and identify academics whose research connects closely with your academic background and interests. 2. Identify Several Potential Topics Do not necessarily limit yourself to one research area. The programme encourages applicants to provide a prioritised list of topics and supervisors they would consider. 3. Check the NERC Remit Make sure at least one proposed research area clearly falls within NERC s remit. 4. Prepare Your 250-Word Research Summary The summary should communicate: What area you want to research Why the area interests you What environmental problem or research question motivates you How your interests relate to the supervisor Why the proposed area is appropriate for environmental science research 5. Request References Early Because two references are required, applicants should approach referees well before the relevant deadline. 6. Check the Exact Course Deadline The CREATES deadline is not necessarily identical across every Cambridge course. Applicants must identify the course associated with their first-choice supervisor and check whether the deadline is 8 December 2026 or 6 January 2027 . 7. Consider Other Cambridge Funding Applicants are encouraged to complete the Cambridge Trust and Gates Cambridge sections where relevant so they can be considered for additional sources of funding. However, some of these schemes have earlier deadlines. Learn more HERE An Opportunity for Environmental Science Researchers The CREATES DLA is designed around major environmental challenges and interdisciplinary scientific research. Its participating departments span areas from Earth sciences and climate research to biodiversity, conservation, genetics, plant sciences, zoology, archaeology and environmental modelling. The programme s broader training environment also aims to develop researchers who can work beyond academia. CREATES has collaborative relationships with organisations across government, industry, conservation and the third sector, creating opportunities for networking and professional development alongside doctoral research. Frequently Asked Questions When does the PhD start? The programme is for students beginning in October 2027 , with the application guidance specifying a 1 October 2027 Michaelmas Term start . How many studentships are available? There are 15 NERC-funded PhD studentships for the 2027 entry. How long is the funding? The studentships are for 3.5 years . Do I need to have a completely finished PhD project before applying? Not necessarily. Applicants identify topics and supervisors, while the final project is intended to be developed with the supervisory team during the first term. Can I apply to supervisors in different departments? Yes. The guidance allows applicants to choose supervisors across more than one department, although applicants should provide a prioritised list. Do I need a research topic within NERC s remit? Yes, if you want to be considered for CREATES NERC DLA funding, at least one proposed topic must fall within the NERC remit. Is an English-language requirement applicable? Yes. Applicants must meet Cambridge s English-language requirements where applicable. When is the application deadline? The applicable CREATES deadline is the same as the funding deadline for the applicant s chosen course: 8 December 2026 or 6 January 2027 . When are interviews expected? Online interviews are anticipated during the week of 22 February 2027 . When will offers be made? Initial offers are expected from late February, with the NERC Universal Acceptance Date at noon on 17 March 2027 . Conclusion The University of Cambridge CREATES NERC-funded PhD Studentships 2027 provide an opportunity for prospective doctoral researchers to pursue advanced environmental science research within one of the world s leading research universities. The programme offers 15 funded 3.5-year PhD studentships , with research opportunities spanning climate change, environmental processes, biology, conservation, Earth sciences, geological hazards and other areas within the NERC remit. Applicants should begin by identifying relevant research topics and supervisors, checking that at least one proposed area falls within NERC s remit, contacting prospective supervisors, preparing their 250-word research summary and arranging their two references well ahead of the deadline. Because the final application deadline depends on the chosen Cambridge course, prospective applicants should check carefully whether their deadline is 8 December 2026 or 6 January 2027 . Early preparation is particularly important for applicants who also want to be considered for other Cambridge funding schemes with earlier deadlines. For applicants with a strong academic background and a clear interest in environmental research, the CREATES DLA provides a structured route toward doctoral research, specialist training and interdisciplinary engagement in areas addressing some of the world s most significant environmental challenges. title: Libra Philanthropies 2027 Rising Global Leaders Changemakers Climate Cohort: 9-Month Leadership Programme for Emerging Climate Leaders
summary: The Libra Philanthropies 2027 Rising Global Leaders (RGL) Changemakers Climate Cohort is now accepting applications from emerging leaders who are already working to advance climate action through community-based initiatives, organizations, or other climate-focused work. The programme is a nine-month leadership development and experiential learning initiative designed to help rising climate leaders strengthen their leadership capabilities, expand their networks, understand the systems shaping climate decisions, and build their ability to create meaningful change within their communities and beyond. Applications opened on September 22, 2026 , and will close on October 23, 2026 . The programme will run from January to September 2027 and will combine in-person convenings, online sessions, peer learning, strategic workshops, experiential learning, and individualized capacity-building support. What Is the 2027 Rising Global Leaders Changemakers Climate Cohort? The Climate Cohort is part of Libra Philanthropies Rising Global Leaders programme, which supports emerging and community-based leaders through leadership development, mentorship, immersive learning, peer exchange, and international networking opportunities. Within the Rising Global Leaders programme, the Changemakers pathway is designed for leaders who already have a clear focus area and are actively creating impact within their communities. The Climate Cohort applies this approach specifically to climate action and community-grounded climate work. The 2027 cohort recognizes that climate change affects much more than the environment. Climate-related decisions can influence: Where people can live How communities develop Economic growth and livelihoods Population displacement Wildlife and ecosystems Energy systems Land use Financial systems Public policy Community resilience Long-term development Libra Philanthropies programme is therefore intended to help emerging leaders better understand the systems, institutions, funding structures, and decision-making environments that influence climate action. Why the Climate Cohort Was Created One of the central ideas behind the programme is the gap between those who experience climate impacts most directly and those who participate in decisions about climate policy and investment . Climate decisions made today can have consequences that extend across generations. Yet emerging leaders who are closest to climate-related challenges may not always have access to the institutions, networks, resources, or decision-making spaces where priorities are established. The Climate Cohort seeks to help address this gap by providing participants with: Knowledge Leadership skills Networks Confidence Organizational capacity Exposure to climate decision-making systems Opportunities for peer learning Experiential learning Connections with other leaders The official programme describes the goal as helping emerging climate leaders navigate the systems influencing climate action and strengthen their ability to create change. Who Is the Climate Cohort Designed For? The programme is intended for climate leaders between the ages of 20 and 35 who are already leading or playing a significant role in a climate-focused initiative or organization. The initiative or organization should: Have been operating for at least one year Be nonpartisan Preferably have an annual budget below $500,000 Address climate change in ways grounded in the needs and experiences of the communities it serves Applicants should also be willing to collaborate, share their experiences, participate in collective learning, and contribute to a broader community of climate leaders. Importantly, the programme is intended for people who are already taking action , rather than individuals who are simply interested in climate change but have no existing climate-focused initiative or organizational role. What Participants Will Learn The 2027 Climate Cohort is organized around three thematic pillars . 1. Understanding the Climate System Participants will explore how different systems influence climate action. This includes examining: Funding Power Institutions Accountability Climate commitments Decision-making The relationship between resources and climate solutions The goal is to help participants understand not only what climate challenges exist, but also how decisions about climate solutions are made and which factors determine whether those solutions receive support . 2. Local Adaptation and Community Resilience The second pillar focuses on the relationship between climate change and people s everyday lives. Participants will examine: How climate change affects communities Community responses to climate challenges Locally led adaptation Resilience-building Community-based approaches to climate action This emphasis reflects the programme s focus on climate initiatives that are grounded in the needs and experiences of communities. 3. Moving From Participation to Climate Action and Influence The third pillar focuses on helping participants translate participation into sustained influence. Participants will develop relationships, strategies, tools, and credibility that can help them advance climate solutions and participate more effectively in spaces where climate priorities are shaped. This includes developing the ability to move from simply participating in climate conversations toward building meaningful influence and sustained action . What Does the 9-Month Programme Include? The Climate Cohort combines several different learning and leadership-development approaches. In-Person Convenings Participants will come together in person three times during the programme . Kickoff — February 2027 The programme begins with an in-person kickoff focused on exploring the foundations of climate action. The location is currently listed as to be determined . Experiential Learning Trip — May 2027 Participants will take part in an experiential learning trip designed to connect the cohort s learning with real-world climate contexts. The destination is also currently listed as to be determined . Concordia Summit and Graduation — September 2027 The programme concludes in New York City , where participants will attend the 2027 Concordia Annual Summit , reflect on their development, graduate from the Climate Cohort, and become part of a broader global leadership community. Strategic Workshops Participants will take part in expert-led workshops that provide both theoretical and practical learning. These workshops are designed to: Deepen participants understanding of climate systems Challenge existing assumptions Introduce practical tools Develop analytical skills Connect climate concepts with real-world work Help participants apply learning directly to their initiatives The workshops will be connected to the programme s three thematic pillars. Personalized Capacity-Building A major component of the programme is individualized support. Participants will receive capacity-building tailored to the needs of the cohort and their work. Areas may include: Strategy Governance Communications Partnership building Leadership Organizational development This means participants will not only learn together as a group but will also have opportunities to strengthen skills relevant to their individual leadership and organizational challenges. Cohort Reflection Circles The Climate Cohort also includes Cohort Reflection Circles . These sessions provide participants with a space to: Share experiences Discuss challenges Exchange ideas Reflect on their work Learn from other participants Explore possible strategies together Build relationships with fellow climate leaders The emphasis is on peer-to-peer learning and honest exchange rather than only formal instruction. RGL Engagement Circles Participants will also have the opportunity to share their knowledge with younger members of the broader Rising Global Leaders community. Through RGL Engagement Circles , Climate Cohort participants, referred to as Changemakers, can lead discussions and workshops for individuals who are at earlier stages of their leadership journeys. This creates an additional opportunity for participants to reflect on their own experiences and contribute to the development of younger emerging leaders. Mentorship, Networking and Global Exposure The Climate Cohort is designed not only as an educational programme but also as a leadership network. The programme provides opportunities for: Mentorship Peer exchange International networking Experiential learning Engagement with other social-impact leaders Connections across different climate initiatives and communities Libra Philanthropies describes Rising Global Leaders as a broader programme intended to connect emerging leaders through mentorship, immersive experiences, and peer-to-peer exchange. The Climate Cohort therefore provides participants with the opportunity to develop relationships beyond their immediate organizations and communities. Programme Time Commitment Participants should expect approximately 100–110 hours of active participation throughout the nine-month programme. This includes: In-person workshops Virtual sessions Reflection circles Independent activities Additional engagements The most intensive periods are expected to coincide with the three in-person gatherings: February: Kickoff, approximately four days May: Experiential/Immersion Trip, approximately four days September: New York City trip and Concordia Summit, approximately three days Participants are expected to attend scheduled sessions in order to fully participate in the programme. Is the Climate Cohort Fully Funded? Yes. According to the official Libra Philanthropies programme page, all travel and programme-related costs will be fully covered by Libra Philanthropies . This is particularly relevant because the programme includes international or multi-location in-person components, including the experiential learning trip and the final New York City gathering. The programme information does not state a separate personal stipend or salary for participants, so applicants should distinguish between covered programme/travel costs and a personal financial award. Apply HERE How Many Participants Will Be Selected? The 2027 Climate Cohort is expected to include 6–8 participants . The small cohort is intended to allow participants to develop deeper relationships, collaborate closely, and receive more tailored support throughout the programme. This makes the application process selective, particularly because the programme is intended for leaders who are already engaged in climate-focused work. Application Process The application process consists of several stages. Step 1: Complete the Online Application Applicants must complete the written application, which takes approximately 30 minutes according to the official programme page. Applicants must also submit a short recorded video introducing themselves and their climate-related work . Step 2: Application Review Libra Philanthropies will review submitted applications against the programme s eligibility and selection criteria. The organization uses a rolling review process as applications are received. Step 3: Interviews Shortlisted candidates will be invited to an interview with members of the programme team. Step 4: Final Selection Selected participants will be notified before the 2027 Climate Cohort is publicly announced. The official timeline lists: Applications open: September 22, 2026 Applications close: October 23, 2026 Rolling application review Shortlisted interviews: November 2026 Final cohort announcement: December 2026 Important Deadline The application deadline for the 2027 Rising Global Leaders Changemakers Climate Cohort is: October 23, 2026. Applicants should complete the written application and recorded video submission before the deadline. What Kind of Climate Work Is Relevant? The programme does not limit applicants to one specific climate discipline. The official eligibility language focuses on climate-focused initiatives or organizations and community-grounded climate work. This can potentially include initiatives working around areas such as: Climate adaptation Community resilience Environmental sustainability Climate policy Climate education Energy Land and natural resources Community development Climate finance Environmental justice Locally led climate solutions However, applicants should ensure that their actual initiative demonstrates a clear connection to climate change and is grounded in the needs and experiences of the communities they serve. What Makes This Opportunity Different? The Climate Cohort is structured around the idea that climate leadership requires more than technical knowledge about climate change. Participants are expected to develop an understanding of the systems surrounding climate action . This includes understanding: Who makes climate decisions How climate priorities are established How funding influences climate solutions How institutions shape action How communities respond to climate impacts How leaders can build influence How organizations can strengthen their strategies How different leaders can collaborate across communities and borders The programme therefore combines leadership development, organizational capacity-building, experiential learning and climate-focused systems thinking . Learn more HERE Why Community-Grounded Leadership Matters A defining feature of the Climate Cohort is its focus on leaders whose climate work is connected to communities. Rather than focusing exclusively on large institutions or established organizations, the programme seeks leaders who are already working within or alongside communities to address climate-related challenges. This reflects the broader philosophy of Libra Philanthropies Rising Global Leaders programme, which describes Changemakers as community-based leaders who understand local challenges firsthand and are already taking action, often with limited resources. About Libra Philanthropies Libra Philanthropies was established in 2023 by the Logothetis family as an independent 501(c)(3) foundation. Its work focuses on developing partnerships, creating programmes, supporting changemakers, and addressing social needs internationally. The organization describes its broader Rising Global Leaders programme as a platform for supporting emerging leaders at different stages of their leadership journeys. How to Prepare a Strong Application Applicants can strengthen their preparation by making sure their application clearly communicates the connection between their leadership, their initiative, their community, and climate action . 1. title: Center for Community Health Equity Accelerator Fellowship 2027: Up to $10,000 in Project Funding and Leadership Support for Community Health Equity Leaders
summary: The Center for Community Health Equity Accelerator Fellowship 2027 is now accepting applications from community leaders with ideas for projects that can advance health equity and address social determinants of health within the M Health Fairview service area. The year-long fellowship is designed to help participants strengthen their leadership, develop their project ideas, receive expert guidance, and turn community-focused ideas into practical action. The program, offered through the M Health Fairview Center for Community Health Equity , combines leadership development, education, coaching, technical assistance, peer learning, networking, and financial support. Each selected fellow can receive up to $10,000 in project funding , in addition to a $3,000 participation stipend intended to help support costs associated with participating in the fellowship. For the 2027 cohort, eight fellows will be selected. The fellowship will run from January through December 2027 , with sessions delivered through a combination of in-person meetings across the seven-county metro area and virtual sessions. What Is the Center for Community Health Equity Accelerator Fellowship? The Accelerator Fellowship is a 12-month leadership development program created to support community leaders who are working on innovative approaches to health equity and the social conditions that influence people s health and wellbeing. Rather than requiring applicants to already have a completely developed project, the fellowship provides space for participants to develop, test, refine, and implement their ideas during the fellowship year. The program is particularly focused on helping community leaders move from an identified community challenge toward a practical project with achievable goals and measurable activities. According to M Health Fairview, fellows receive structured support to: Build and strengthen leadership capacity Sharpen their vision for community change Develop and refine a health equity project Receive coaching and technical assistance Learn about health equity and project implementation Connect with other community leaders Develop partnerships and community relationships Put their project ideas into action Receive financial resources to support project implementation Each fellow will be part of a cohort of eight community leaders who learn and grow together throughout the year. Up to $10,000 in Project Funding One of the major components of the 2027 Accelerator Fellowship is financial support for fellows community projects. Each fellow can receive up to $10,000 in project funding to help bring their health equity project to life. Importantly, applicants do not need to have a fully developed project when they apply. The fellowship provides the full year for fellows to build, test, and refine their approaches with support from coaches, experts, and peers. The application specifically asks applicants to explain how the project funding will support their proposed activities and requires a draft project budget outlining expected expenses of up to $10,000. In addition to project funding, the official FAQ states that fellows receive a $3,000 stipend to support participation in the fellowship. This may help cover costs such as compensation for time, transportation, childcare, or other incidental expenses. ( mhealthfairview.org ) What Does the Fellowship Provide? The Accelerator Fellowship offers several forms of support throughout the year. 1. Health Equity Education Fellows participate in an educational curriculum covering health equity, program development, implementation, and related areas of community work. The curriculum is designed to give participants both conceptual knowledge and practical tools that they can apply to their projects. 2. Coaching and Technical Assistance Participants receive coaching and technical assistance from experts working in relevant fields. This allows fellows to receive guidance while developing their projects, addressing challenges, refining their approaches, and moving from ideas toward implementation. 3. Project Funding Fellows receive up to $10,000 to support implementation of their health equity projects. This funding is intended to help participants turn their ideas into practical community initiatives rather than simply developing theoretical proposals. 4. Networking and Peer Learning The fellowship creates opportunities for participants to build relationships with other community leaders and professionals whose interests align with their work. Because the eight fellows progress through the program together, the cohort provides an environment for shared learning, collaboration, and exchange of different perspectives. What Types of Projects Can Applicants Propose? The fellowship is focused on projects that address health equity or social determinants of health within the eligible service area. A project does not necessarily need to be a traditional healthcare project. Health equity can involve the broader conditions that influence people s ability to live healthy lives, including issues involving housing, food, education, community connection, environment, access to resources, and other structural or social factors. The 2026 cohort illustrates the breadth of projects that can fit within the program. Previous fellows worked on initiatives involving culturally responsive nutrition, community barbering and mentorship, rural wellness, housing stability, Indigenous food and knowledge systems, transitional housing and recovery, and grief and trauma education. This demonstrates that applicants can approach health equity from different professional, cultural, community, and disciplinary perspectives. What Makes a Strong Project Idea? According to the fellowship s published criteria, a strong project should be community-rooted , meaning that it responds to a real and identified need within a specific community and demonstrates community engagement in shaping the idea. The project should also be equity-focused , with the goal of reducing health disparities or addressing structural barriers to equity. Applicants should also demonstrate that their project is: Realistic Actionable Appropriately scoped for the fellowship period Supported by achievable objectives Based on a reasonable budget Connected to an identified community need The program also states that it values diversity of perspective over formal titles , meaning applicants are not required to rely solely on conventional professional credentials to demonstrate their ability to contribute. ( mhealthfairview.org ) Who Is the Fellowship Looking For? The Accelerator Fellowship is designed for community leaders , and applicants can come from different professional backgrounds and career stages. The published FAQ states that applicants from all backgrounds, professions, and career stages are welcome. The fellowship looks for individuals who have contributed to their communities professionally or personally and who demonstrate commitment to health equity. ( mhealthfairview.org ) Applicants are expected to demonstrate qualities such as: Community orientation Commitment to health equity Collaboration Resourcefulness Commitment to participating fully Authenticity Openness and curiosity A solution-oriented approach The fellowship is specifically for individual applicants rather than organizations . ( mhealthfairview.org ) Eligibility Requirements for the 2027 Cohort Applicants must meet the following requirements: Have a project idea focused on advancing health equity in their community. Plan to implement the project within Fairview s service area. Be at least 18 years old. Not currently be employed by Fairview Health Services. Have related experience, relationships, or community ties to the issue or topic they want to address. Be available to attend all required fellowship sessions. The program is therefore not simply looking for people with an interesting idea. Applicants should be able to demonstrate some meaningful relationship with the issue or community they want to serve. Where Must the Project Be Implemented? A particularly important eligibility requirement is geography. The project must be implemented within the M Health Fairview service area . The published eligible counties are: Minnesota Anoka Benton Carver Chisago Dakota Hennepin Isanti Itasca Kanabec Mille Lacs Pine Ramsey Saint Louis Scott Sherburne Washington Wright Wisconsin Pierce County Saint Croix County Therefore, this is not an open worldwide fellowship . The proposed project must be located within the specified M Health Fairview service-area geography. ( mhealthfairview.org ) Fellowship Duration and Format The 2027 Accelerator Fellowship runs for 12 months, from January through December 2027 . Sessions will combine: In-person sessions Virtual sessions Workshops Learning activities Leadership development Project work Coaching Peer learning Most months will include two sessions, which may consist of full-day in-person meetings or shorter virtual sessions. The published FAQ estimates approximately 105 hours of in-class time over the fellowship, in addition to the time fellows need to spend implementing their individual projects. ( mhealthfairview.org ) Areas Covered by the Fellowship Curriculum The program s curriculum is designed to develop both leadership and practical project-management capabilities. Topics include: Orientation and foundations Funding and evaluation Project planning Project management Strategic communications Community engagement Community mapping and collaboration Public health, policy, environment and systems change Leadership and partnerships Learning and coaching Reflection and sharing Celebration and showcase The curriculum can adapt to the needs of the cohort, and the organizers note that session topics may change. ( mhealthfairview.org ) Application Requirements Applicants should prepare several components before submitting the application. The required materials include: Basic personal information Two letters of recommendation Narrative responses to the application questions Additional information about the proposed project A draft project budget If the proposed project is affiliated with an organization, at least one recommendation/support letter should come from that organization. Applicants should also download and review the full application and budget template before completing the online application. The application process involves: Reviewing the full application form. Reviewing and completing the draft budget template. Completing the online application. Uploading two recommendation/support letters. Uploading the draft budget. Submitting the complete application before the deadline. Application Questions The application asks applicants to explain both their health equity vision and their leadership journey . Your Vision for Health Equity Applicants are asked to explain: What health equity challenge they want to address Why the issue matters to their community What has contributed to their understanding of the issue Why they are personally positioned to address it What transformation they hope to achieve What impact they intend to make What their proposed project involves How the $10,000 project funding would support the work Their three primary objectives for the fellowship period The application places a 1,500-character limit on the problem, proposal, and objectives responses. Your Leadership Journey Applicants are also asked to discuss their leadership experience and how their background, identity, relationships, and life experiences have shaped their approach to leadership. The application allows applicants to provide examples of formal or informal leadership and explain how their leadership journey connects to their proposed project. This section has a 2,000-character limit or a three-minute video option , with applicants choosing one format. Applicants are additionally asked how the fellowship could support their leadership development, what they could contribute to the cohort, why the timing is appropriate, and what skills, resources, or technical assistance would help them achieve their health equity vision. Selection and Number of Fellows The 2027 fellowship will select eight applicants . The selection process is competitive. Semi-finalists are expected to be notified in late October and invited to participate in an interview in early November. The interview can be conducted virtually if needed. Final cohort selections are expected to be announced in mid-November, with all applicants notified of final decisions by late November. Important Application Deadline The deadline for the Center for Community Health Equity Accelerator Fellowship 2027 is: Thursday, October 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. CST. Applicants should ensure that the complete application, required recommendation letters, and draft budget are submitted before the deadline. Is This a Scholarship or a Grant? The Accelerator Fellowship is structured primarily as a leadership development fellowship with project funding , rather than a traditional academic scholarship. The program combines: Leadership development Health equity education Coaching Technical assistance Peer networking Project implementation support Up to $10,000 in project funding A $3,000 participation stipend It is also not a degree or credit-bearing academic program. ( mhealthfairview.org ) Why This Fellowship May Be Relevant to Community Leaders The fellowship is designed around the idea that many health challenges cannot be addressed through healthcare services alone. Community conditions, social environments, access to resources, housing, food, education, relationships, and other factors can influence health outcomes. M Health Fairview s Center for Community Health Equity works with community partners to address these broader determinants and reduce disparities. ( mhealthfairview.org ) The Accelerator Fellowship therefore provides a structured environment in which community leaders can develop projects that respond to issues they understand through direct community experience. The combination of project funding and leadership development also allows fellows to work on both sides of the challenge: strengthening their own capacity as leaders while developing a practical response to a community health equity issue. Tips for Preparing a Strong Application Applicants should pay close attention to the relationship between their community, problem, project, leadership experience, and proposed outcomes . A strong application should clearly explain: 1. The community problem Identify a specific health equity challenge rather than describing a broad social issue without context. 2. Why the problem matters Explain how the issue affects the community and why addressing it is important. 3. Your connection to the issue The fellowship specifically asks applicants to demonstrate related experience, relationships, or community ties. 4. Your proposed solution Explain what you want to do and how the project would address the identified problem. 5. Your objectives Define three realistic objectives that can be pursued between January and December 2027. 6. Your use of funding Show how the proposed $10,000 would directly support project activities. 7. Your leadership story The application is interested not only in the project but also in the person leading it. Explain how your experiences have shaped your approach to leadership. 8. Your readiness Because fellows are expected to participate throughout the year, applicants should demonstrate that they can commit to the program s sessions and project implementation requirements. Learn more HERE Conclusion The Center for Community Health Equity Accelerator Fellowship 2027 provides a year-long opportunity for community leaders to develop health equity projects while strengthening their leadership skills and community connections. The program combines education, coaching, technical assistance, networking, and financial support, with each fellow eligible for up to $10,000 in project funding and a $3,000 participation stipend . ( mhealthfairview.org ) The fellowship is particularly focused on individuals who understand a community health equity challenge through their experience, relationships, or community ties and who have an idea they want to develop into practical action. Eight fellows will be selected for the 2027 cohort, which will run from January through December 2027. Applicants should carefully review the geographic requirements because projects must be implemented within the specified M Health Fairview service area. The application deadline is October 1, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. CST . Who Can Apply? Category of qualifying people: Individual community leaders aged 18 or older with a health equity project idea and a meaningful connection to the issue or community they intend to serve. Key qualifications Applicants must: Be at least 18 years old. Have a project idea focused on advancing health equity. Have related experience, relationships, or community ties to the issue. Plan to implement the project within the eligible M Health Fairview service area. Be available to participate in all required fellowship sessions. Not currently be employed by Fairview Health Services. Apply as an individual rather than as an organization. Applicants may come from different professions, backgrounds, and career stages ; the program states that diversity of perspective is valued over formal titles. ( mhealthfairview.org ) Apply for the 2027 Accelerator Fellowship View the official M Health Fairview fellowship information MORE OPPORTUNITIES HERE The post Center for Community Health Equity Accelerator Fellowship 2027: Up to $10,000 in Project Funding and Leadership Support for Community Health Equity Leaders appeared first on Opportunities for Youth .

title: Education Endowment Foundation Research Funding Opportunities: Three Calls for Research Proposals in England’s Education Sector
summary: The Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) has announced three research opportunities inviting legally constituted organisations and research teams to submit proposals examining important issues in education across England. The calls focus on inclusive mainstream education and Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), technical and vocational teaching for learners aged 16–19, and the continuity of exam boards for GCSE resit learners. These opportunities are particularly relevant to education research organisations, universities, research consultancies, policy institutes, and research consortia with expertise in qualitative research, education, pedagogy, impact evaluation, process evaluation, and the 16–19 education sector. The three calls seek to generate evidence that can contribute to future EEF guidance, research commissioning, and education policy. Depending on the opportunity, successful research teams may be expected to conduct school or college visits, classroom observations, quantitative analysis, qualitative research, feasibility work, or evaluation activities. Below is a detailed overview of all three EEF research opportunities, including their objectives, research questions, methodological expectations, eligibility requirements, and application deadlines. 1. Practice Review on the Inclusive Mainstream Fund and Inclusion Strategies The Education Endowment Foundation is commissioning a practice review examining how schools in England are developing inclusion strategies and approaching their use of the Inclusive Mainstream Fund (IMF). The research comes at a time of significant policy development around creating a more inclusive mainstream education system in England, particularly for children and young people with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities. Background and Context The Government’s 2026 Schools White Paper set out an ambition to create a more inclusive mainstream education system in which schools are appropriately equipped and funded to support children with SEND to achieve and thrive within inclusive mainstream settings. As part of this broader reform agenda, the Department for Education has committed to a package of measures intended to strengthen inclusion within mainstream schools. One of these measures is the Inclusive Mainstream Fund. In addition, the Department for Education expects all state-maintained mainstream schools to develop and publish an inclusion strategy on their websites by 31 December each year. These developments create an opportunity to understand how schools are responding to the new expectations in practice. The EEF therefore wants to build an evidence base around how schools are developing their inclusion strategies and making decisions concerning the Inclusive Mainstream Fund. What the Inclusive Mainstream Fund Research Will Examine The practice review aims to develop a clearer picture of current practice across different school settings. In particular, the research will: Map current approaches to developing inclusion strategies across school settings. Examine how schools are approaching spending through the Inclusive Mainstream Fund. Explore differences in practice between schools and settings. Investigate reported changes in behaviours and beliefs associated with the introduction of the new policies. Explore changes in decision-making that may be connected to the new inclusion policies. Identify emerging approaches that may be relevant to future EEF guidance and research. The research is therefore not simply focused on whether schools have developed inclusion strategies. It is also concerned with understanding the processes behind those strategies and how schools are making decisions about resources and inclusion. How the Research Findings Will Be Used The findings from this research are expected to have several applications within education policy, research and practice. The evidence may inform future development of EEF guidance relating to inclusion, including resources such as the EEF Guide to Inclusive Teaching. The findings may also contribute to: Future EEF research activity. The development of additional evidence-based resources. Understanding of emerging practices in mainstream schools. Advice provided to policymakers. Future research priorities concerning inclusive education and SEND. The main output from the project will be a written research report. The report is expected to be published by the end of March 2027. Research Approach The EEF welcomes proposals capable of addressing both the primary and secondary research questions. Applicants are encouraged to consider a variety of research methods and may propose innovative approaches where appropriate. A mixed-methods approach may be suitable for the project, depending on the proposed research questions and methodology. Applicants should therefore demonstrate clearly how their proposed methodology will allow them to develop a meaningful understanding of: How schools are developing inclusion strategies. How schools are approaching Inclusive Mainstream Fund spending. Whether behaviours and beliefs are changing. How decision-making may be changing in response to the policies. How practices vary between different school settings. Who Can Apply for the Inclusive Mainstream Fund Practice Review? The opportunity is primarily relevant to organisations and research teams with expertise in education research, particularly research involving schools, inclusion, SEND, policy implementation, and qualitative or mixed-methods research. Potential applicants may include: Universities and higher education institutions. Education research organisations. Research consultancies. Policy research organisations. Specialist education research teams. Consortia bringing together complementary research expertise. Applicants should carefully review the complete EEF invitation to tender and selection criteria before submitting a proposal. Deadline for the Inclusive Mainstream Fund Research Opportunity Completed applications must be submitted through the designated Form Assembly application form by: 12pm on Monday, 19 October 2026. Applicants should allow sufficient time to review the tender documentation, prepare their methodology and supporting information, and complete the online submission before the deadline. APPLY HERE 2. Practice Review on 16–19 Technical and Vocational Teaching The second EEF research opportunity focuses on teaching practices within technical and vocational education for learners aged 16–19. The research will investigate current teaching approaches across technical and vocational subject areas and examine how these practices relate to the Initial Teacher Training and Early Career Framework (ITTECF) used in schools. The project is intended to provide a clearer understanding of what teaching currently looks like in technical and vocational settings. Project Summary The practice review will involve detailed observations of teaching practice across a selection of technical and vocational subject areas in the 16–19 sector. Researchers will examine teaching in classrooms and workshops to build a picture of current practice. The research is expected to contribute to understanding: The teaching approaches currently being used. How frequently particular teaching practices are observed. Whether practices identified in the schools ITTECF are also used in technical and vocational education. Whether technical and vocational teachers use other teaching approaches that are not represented in the ITTECF. Whether there are common patterns among colleges that perform particularly well for learners in the identified subject areas. The findings may subsequently inform future EEF research commissioning and guidance for the technical and vocational education sector. Main Research Aims The project has several interconnected aims. 1. Understand Current Teaching Practice The research will examine teaching practices currently being used in technical and vocational education settings. This is intended to provide a practical snapshot of teaching across relevant 16–19 settings. 2. Examine Use of ITTECF Teaching Practices Researchers will investigate whether teaching practices identified within the schools Initial Teacher Training and Early Career Framework are being used in technical and vocational education. The research will also consider whether some of these practices are more prevalent than others. 3. Identify Additional Teaching Practices The project will look beyond the practices contained in the ITTECF. Researchers will identify whether there are other teaching practices commonly observed in technical and vocational education that are not included within the ITTECF framework. 4. Explore High-Performing Colleges The research will also examine whether colleges performing particularly well for learners in the identified subject areas demonstrate common approaches to teaching. This could include investigating whether successful colleges use particular combinations or amounts of the identified teaching practices. Main Research Question The central research question is: Do vocational and technical teachers use the teaching practices identified from the schools ITTECF in their day-to-day teaching? This question will provide the foundation for the practice review. Secondary Research Questions The research will also investigate several related questions, including: Are some of the teaching practices more prevalent than others? Are other teaching practices observed that are not included in the ITTECF? Do colleges that perform particularly well for learners in the identified subject areas use different combinations of the teaching practices? Do these high-performing colleges use different amounts of particular teaching practices? Answering these questions will help the EEF understand whether teaching approaches used in technical and vocational education closely resemble those used in schools or whether there are distinctive practices within the 16–19 sector. Methodological Expectations The project will involve primary research intended to provide a snapshot of current teaching practice in vocational and technical education for learners aged 16–19. The EEF is open to proposals using different research methodologies. Applicants are encouraged to propose approaches that can effectively answer the primary and secondary research questions. Innovative research approaches are also welcomed. However, college visits and observations are expected to be a key component of the research plan. This means applicants should carefully consider how their proposed methodology will allow researchers to observe teaching directly within technical and vocational settings. Feasibility Phase Proposals are expected to include a short feasibility phase. This feasibility phase should involve a small number of colleges and will help researchers test: The suitability of the subject areas identified for the research. The proposed list of classroom teaching practices. The practicality of the observation approach. Whether the proposed research design can generate useful data. Including a feasibility phase will allow the research team to refine its approach before implementing the broader practice review. Who Should Apply? The EEF is seeking research teams with: Experience conducting qualitative research in education. A strong understanding of the 16–19 education sector. Knowledge of pedagogy in England. Experience designing and implementing education research. The ability to conduct research within colleges and technical or vocational education settings. Applications can be submitted by either a single research team or a consortium. Consortia may be particularly appropriate where different organisations can contribute complementary expertise. However, a consortium must be able to demonstrate that its members can work effectively together and maintain the quality and efficiency of the research project. Organisations Eligible to Apply This opportunity is open to legally constituted organisations rather than individuals. Importantly, applicants do not have to be members of the EEF s existing panel of evaluators. The organisation also does not necessarily have to be based in England. International organisations may apply, provided they can demonstrate that: Their research outputs will be relevant to the English education system. The proposed research team has sufficient understanding of the English 16–19 education context. The proposal represents value for money. The organisation has the appropriate legal constitution to undertake the work. This makes the opportunity potentially relevant to eligible education research organisations outside England, provided they can demonstrate appropriate knowledge and contextual expertise. Deadline for the 16–19 Technical and Vocational Teaching Research Opportunity Interested applicants must submit their full research proposals by: 5pm on Friday, 16 October 2026. Questions relating to the tender and research proposals should be directed to the EEF contact provided in the original tender documentation. Research proposals should be sent to: post-16@eefoundation.org.uk 3. 16–19 Setting Choices: GCSE Resit Exam Board Continuity The third opportunity focuses on GCSE resits among learners aged 16–19 in England. The EEF is seeking research proposals to investigate whether maintaining the same exam board between a learner s original GCSE sitting and their subsequent GCSE resit is associated with differences in English and mathematics outcomes. This research forms part of the EEF s Setting Choices programme. Overview of the GCSE Resit Research The project will investigate whether sitting a GCSE resit with the same examination board used for the learner s initial GCSE sitting affects outcomes in English and mathematics. The research will compare continuity with changing exam boards. The central issue is whether maintaining the same examination board provides any measurable difference in outcomes for learners undertaking GCSE resits between the ages of 16 and 19. Background to the Research The research takes place against a wider concern about attainment differences during the 16–19 phase of education. According to the background information provided by the EEF, the socio-economic attainment gap is particularly significant during the 16–19 phase. The Education Policy Institute s 2026 annual report reported that the 16–19 disadvantage gap had remained broadly stable at approximately 3.3–3.4 grades, reaching 3.4 grades in 2025. The EEF describes the 16–19 phase as an important opportunity to improve attainment and strengthen young people s future life chances. Within this broader context, the EEF is interested in examining factors that could potentially influence the success of GCSE resit learners. Why Exam Board Continuity Is Being Studied The choice of examination board may influence aspects of a learner s resit experience. The EEF s research background notes that some colleges deliberately align examination boards with feeder schools for English, mathematics, or both. Other colleges do not maintain this alignment. The rationale for continuity is that learners may benefit from familiarity with the examination structure and expectations associated with the same exam board. At the same time, changing examination boards could potentially offer a learner a different approach. The purpose of the proposed research is not to assume that one approach is beneficial, but to generate evidence about whether continuity is associated with differences in English and mathematics outcomes. Existing Evidence and Rationale The EEF s background information references the Education Policy Institute s Drivers of Success report, which identified examination board choice and continuity with a learner s original examination board as potentially relevant to GCSE resit success. The EEF has also surveyed its college network, consisting of approximately 90 colleges. The survey found that some colleges deliberately align examination boards with feeder schools, while others do not use such alignment. This variation in practice provides an opportunity to investigate the issue through research. Main Research Question The central research question is: Does sitting a GCSE resit with the same exam board as the initial sitting, compared with using a different exam board, affect English and mathematics outcomes for 16–19 resit learners? The research is expected to provide evidence capable of assessing the relationship between examination board continuity and learner outcomes. Expected Research Design The EEF expects the research to include several important components. 1. Causal Impact Evaluation The project is expected to include a causal impact evaluation using a quasi-experimental design. This component is intended to investigate whether differences in exam board continuity are associated with differences in learner outcomes while addressing relevant methodological challenges. 2. Implementation and Process Evaluation A light-touch Implementation and Process Evaluation is also expected. This component can help researchers understand how exam board continuity operates in practice and provide context for interpreting the impact evaluation findings. 3. Subgroup Analysis The research is also expected to include subgroup analysis of disadvantaged learners. This will allow researchers to investigate whether the relationship between exam board continuity and outcomes differs for learners experiencing disadvantage. Who Should Apply? The EEF is inviting research teams with experience conducting: Impact evaluations. Process evaluations. Education research. Research within the 16–19 sector. Quasi-experimental research. Quantitative analysis of learner outcomes. The EEF is interested in expressions of interest from individual research teams as well as consortia with complementary expertise. Consortia should demonstrate that their members can work effectively together to ensure the quality and efficiency of the research. Organisational Eligibility Applications are accepted from legally constituted organisations rather than individuals. Researchers do not need to be members of the EEF s panel of evaluators. Organisations based outside England are also eligible to apply. However, international organisations must demonstrate that their teams possess the knowledge and expertise necessary to undertake research relevant to the English education system and complete the proposed work effectively. Deadline for the GCSE Resit Exam Board Continuity Opportunity Interested applicants must submit their Expression of Interest through the designated application form by: 5pm on Monday, 12 October 2026. Applicants should ensure that their EOI addresses the requirements specified in the EEF tender documentation and demonstrates the research team s relevant expertise. Comparison of the Three EEF Research Opportunities Although all three opportunities are focused on education research, they address different areas of the English education system. Opportunity Main Focus Key Research Approach Eligible Applicants Deadline Inclusive Mainstream Fund and Inclusion Strategies Inclusion strategies and IMF spending in mainstream schools Practice review; potentially mixed methods Eligible research organisations/teams 12pm, 19 October 2026 16–19 Technical and Vocational Teaching Teaching practices in technical and vocational education Primary research, college visits and observations Legally constituted organisations 5pm, 16 October 2026 GCSE Resit Exam Board Continuity Effect of maintaining the same GCSE exam board Quasi-experimental impact evaluation plus process evaluation Legally constituted research organisations 5pm, 12 October 2026 What Applicants Should Consider Before Applying Researchers considering any of these EEF opportunities should carefully examine the specific tender documentation before preparing an application. A strong proposal should be closely aligned with the research questions and methodological expectations of the relevant call. Applicants should consider demonstrating: Relevant Research Expertise The research team should clearly explain its previous experience conducting research relevant to the specific opportunity. For example, applicants for the technical and vocational teaching review should demonstrate knowledge of qualitative education research, pedagogy and the 16–19 sector. Applicants for the GCSE resit project should demonstrate appropriate impact and process evaluation experience. Knowledge of the English Education System International applicants should pay particular attention to demonstrating their understanding of the English education system. The EEF explicitly indicates that organisations based outside England can apply, but they must demonstrate that their research will be relevant to England and that their teams have the necessary knowledge. Appropriate Methodology Proposals should directly address the research questions. Depending on the opportunity, applicants may need to demonstrate expertise in: Qualitative research. Quantitative research. Mixed-methods research. Classroom observation. College visits. Quasi-experimental designs. Impact evaluation. Implementation and process evaluation. Subgroup analysis. Feasibility studies. Collaboration and Consortia Organisations applying as a consortium should clearly establish how responsibilities will be divided and how the partners will work together. The EEF is interested in consortia that bring complementary expertise while maintaining efficient project management and research quality. Relevance and Value for Money Applicants should demonstrate how the proposed work will contribute useful evidence and represent value for money. APPLY HERE Important Deadlines at a Glance Researchers interested in these opportunities should take note of the three deadlines: 12 October 2026, 5pm 16–19 Setting Choices – GCSE Resit Exam Board Continuity 16 October 2026, 5pm 16–19 Technical and Vocational Teaching Practice Review 19 October 2026, 12pm Inclusive Mainstream Fund and Inclusion Strategies Practice Review Because the deadlines occur within a single week, applicants interested in multiple opportunities should begin preparing their submissions well in advance. Who Qualifies for These EEF Opportunities? The opportunities are primarily intended for legally constituted organisations and research teams , rather than individual applicants. Relevant applicants may include: Universities and higher education institutions. Education research organisations. Research institutes. Policy research organisations. Research consultancies. Specialist education research organisations. Consortia combining complementary research expertise. For the Inclusive Mainstream Fund and Inclusion Strategies review, applicants should have relevant expertise in education research, inclusion, SEND, school practice, policy implementation, qualitative research, mixed-methods research, or related areas. For the 16–19 Technical and Vocational Teaching review, applicants should have experience conducting qualitative education research and a strong understanding of the 16–19 sector and pedagogy in England. For the GCSE Resit Exam Board Continuity evaluation, applicants should have experience conducting impact and process evaluations, particularly within the 16–19 education sector. Countries and Regions The calls are focused on the education system in England , but organisations do not necessarily have to be physically based in England. The EEF states that organisations based outside England may apply for the relevant opportunities, provided they can demonstrate the knowledge and expertise required to conduct research relevant to the English education system. Accordingly, eligible organisations may potentially apply from England, elsewhere in the United Kingdom, or other countries , subject to the specific requirements of the applicable tender and the organisation s ability to demonstrate relevant expertise and value for money. These are institutional research opportunities rather than individual scholarships, fellowships or internships , so applicants should apply through an eligible organisation rather than as an individual researcher. Conclusion The Education Endowment Foundation s three new research opportunities provide organisations with the opportunity to contribute evidence to important questions affecting education in England. The first opportunity focuses on inclusive mainstream education , examining how schools are developing inclusion strategies and approaching the Inclusive Mainstream Fund. The research is intended to strengthen understanding of current practice and inform future guidance, research and policy. The second opportunity examines technical and vocational teaching among learners aged 16–19 . Researchers will observe teaching practice across selected subject areas and investigate how teaching approaches in technical and vocational settings compare with practices identified in the Initial Teacher Training and Early Career Framework. The third opportunity focuses on GCSE resit exam board continuity , investigating whether maintaining the same examination board between a learner s initial GCSE sitting and their resit affects English and mathematics outcomes. The project is expected to use a quasi-experimental impact evaluation alongside a light-touch implementation and process evaluation and subgroup analysis of disadvantaged learners. For organisations with relevant research expertise, these calls offer opportunities to undertake research with potential relevance to education practice, evidence-based guidance and policymaking in England. Applicants should carefully review the full tender requirements, ensure that their proposed methodology directly addresses the relevant research questions, and submit their applications before the applicable deadline.
